d: What Ghost Messaging is, and where to start.
x: Ghost Messaging is one app for the people you talk to: your texts, your friends on Ghost, your circles with their chats, calls and files, and your Telegram, Signal and other chats, side by side. Messages between Ghost apps are sealed end to end, there are no ads, and the app is open source. Ghost Messaging is in alpha It works well enough to use every day, but things still change quickly and some features are marked Coming soon . If you're testing it, start with Join the alpha , and tell us anything odd in the Alpha testers circle. Start here Install the app Android, Mac, Windows or Linux, and what to say yes to. Your texts on a computer Pair the Mac, Windows or Linux app with your phone. Build a plugin Make your own, try it in Developer mode, and submit it. Finding your way around Everything starts from the rail down the left of the screen, the same on every page, as Discord and Slack have. At its head is Messages , your conversations. Under it are your circles , each as its picture: tap one to open it, and a halo in its colour marks the one that's open. A dot beside a circle means something's unread; a red number means someone mentioned you. The circled plus under them starts a new circle or joins one by its link. At the foot: New (start a conversation, a group, a space or a circle), Contacts , Archive , the Marketplace (plugins, as a store) and Settings . Hold a pointer over any of them for its name. Right-click one, or press and hold it on a phone, for its menu: a circle's has its settings and members, Archive's marks everything in it read, and the Marketplace's and Settings' jump to a section. A few words we use Word What it means Circle A group of people with a sidebar of spaces, a bit like a small server. You can be in as many as you like. Space A room in a circle (or on its own): chat and voice, text only, files, or an SMS space for people without the app. Friend Someone you talk to over Ghost rather than by text: added by their username, or by their number once you've sealed your texts together. Connections Your other chat accounts linked into Ghost: Telegram, Signal, WhatsApp, Matrix. Routes How messages travel between Ghost apps: over the relay, or by text. Plugin An extra you add from the Marketplace : for yourself, or, built in, for everyone in a circle. On which devices Android phone : everything, including your texts (SMS and picture messages). Mac, Windows and Linux : friends, circles, calls, files and your other chats on their own, and your texts when paired with your Android phone. iPhone Coming soon : friends, circles and calls. d: Recovery words, your password, the account address, and being the same you on every device.
x: You don't need any of this to use Ghost Messaging. It's here for when you want to know what your account is, where it's kept, and what happens when you sign in somewhere else. One identity, on every device Your account is a key that's yours alone, made from your 12 recovery words. Every device you sign in on becomes that same you: your friends see one person, a circle sees one member, and everything sent to you reaches each of your devices. Your username (like @alex ) is how friends find you. It points at your key. Your password unlocks a sealed backup of your key, so you can sign in with a username and password instead of the words. Your 12 recovery words are the key. They work without the password, and nothing else can replace them. The account address The address that starts with 0x , shown when your account is made and in Settings › Me › Account , is your account's public name. It's the same in any wallet app that takes your 12 words, because it's made from them in the same standard way. Ghost doesn't use it for money; it's simply the one name your account has everywhere. Sharing it is safe; sharing your words is not. What the server keeps The relay server at gogho.st keeps your username and a backup of your key, sealed with your password, which is stretched on your device first. The server can't open it. It never sees your recovery words, your password, or your messages. d: What a plugin of your own can do, what it is made of, and how it reaches the Marketplace.
x: A plugin of your own sorts texts the way you'd like them sorted: bills in a tab of their own with the amount on the row, a parcel's tracking number a press away, receipts marked read as they come. It's one file you write by hand that says what to look for in a text and what to do with it. You try it on your own device in Developer mode, then send it to the Marketplace, where it's reviewed before anyone else can add it. What a plugin can do Tag texts by their words : "your bill is ready", "amount due $45.20", a tracking number. A tag can keep what it found, like the amount. Give texts a tab of their own beside Messages and Codes, or a kind in the list's filter that people show or hide. Draw its texts' rows : a value large on the row (the amount, a tracking number), a short caption, a face with a letter and a colour, and a button at the row's end. Add buttons : lines in a conversation's menu in the list, a button in a conversation's header, lines in a message's menu. A button can say something, copy words to the clipboard, write a reply for you to send, mark the conversation read, move it to one of the plugin's tabs or back to Messages, or open the plugin's own web page. Act as texts come : mark texts in its own tabs and kinds as read, or take their notification away, but only behind a switch in its settings that starts off. Have settings of its own : switches, choices, and words the person types (more words for bills, say), shown on its page in the Marketplace. What it can't do It can't reach the internet, and it isn't code: nothing in it runs. It's a description the app follows. A button you press can open its one web page in your browser, and that's all. It never sees your contacts' texts, group texts, texts sent with Ghost Messaging's encryption, your own messages, chats on other networks (Telegram, Signal and the rest), or circles and spaces. It never acts on a text with a sign-in code in it. It can tag one, but never sort it into a tab, mark it read or silence it. It can't change the words of a message, or who a conversation is from: a row always keeps the conversation's own name. It's for you alone, on one device. Plugins from other developers can't be turned on for a whole circle yet. One file: ghost-plugin/1 A plugin is one file, id .ghostplugin , of JSON in the ghost-plugin/1 format: its name and description, its icon, what it may do, its settings, and its rules. It finds words in a text with phrases like amount due {amount} , never with code or regular expressions, so no plugin can hang the app, and one that's slow is paused. Every field is on The plugin file . { "format": "ghost-plugin/1", "id": "mybills", "version": "1.0.0", "name": "My bills", "tagline": "Bills in a tab of their own", "description": "Texts that say a bill is ready go to a Bills tab, with the amount on the row.", "symbol": "calculator", "hue": "amber", "shelf": "organise", "labels": ["bills"], "permissions": ["sort"], "rules": { "tags": [{"tag": "bill", "any": ["your bill is ready", "amount due {amount}"], "detail": {"from": "token"}}], "sections": [{"key": "bills", "label": "Bills", "icon": "calculator", "kind": "tab", "takes": {"tagged": ["bill"]}, "row": {"value": "{tag:bill}"}}] } } That's a whole plugin, as small as one can be: Developer mode loads it as it is. To submit it, it also needs an icon, your username and a help address ( the whole Bills file has them). Where it runs An Android phone : everything, as your texts come. A computer paired with an Android phone : it sorts the phone's texts there too, once it's added on the computer (plugins are added on each device on its own). Marking read and silencing as texts come happen on the phone only. A Mac or Windows PC on its own has no texts, so a plugin does nothing there. iPhone : plugins from other developers aren't on iPhone at all, because of the App Store's rules for apps that add other developers' features. Developer mode can still load your own there, to try it with Try it . From an idea to the Marketplace Write it Start from one of the examples below and change it, or write one from nothing with The plugin file beside you. Any text editor will do. Try it in Developer mode Load it in Settings › Developer › Plugins in development from a file, a link or the clipboard, then try it on a text without waiting for one to come. Change it, press Reload , try it again. Your first plugin walks through it. Submit it Marketplace › Submit a plugin : the plugin, its icon, description and tags, a screenshot or two, and a note for the reviewer. Submit it to the Marketplace . Review A person at Ghost Messaging reads the whole file, tries it, and approves it, asks for changes or turns it down. Marketplace › My submissions shows where it stands, and the app tells you when that changes. Listed Approved, it's in Discover for everyone with the Reviewed mark, under your username. People see what it can do before they add it, and can report it from its page. The examples Two complete plugins to start from, each one file: Example What it shows Bills An amount found in a text and shown large on its row, a tab and a kind, a setting of the person's own words, and marking receipts read behind a switch. Parcels Words between words, tracking codes, a choice setting, a reply to send, a link, moving a conversation back to Messages, and silencing behind a switch. They're on this site at https://gogho.st/docs/examples/bills.ghostplugin and https://gogho.st/docs/examples/parcels.ghostplugin , which Developer mode can load as they are, and in the app's repository in examples/plugins on GitHub , with a note on each. Their ids, bills and parcels , can't be submitted: give yours an id of its own.

d: Tags, tabs and kinds with their rows, buttons and menu lines, and what happens as texts arrive.
x: A plugin's rules say what it does: tags it gives texts by their words, sections (tabs and kinds) that take tagged texts, actions (buttons and menu lines) and incoming rules for texts as they come. Any of them can say when it applies with a condition. The examples here are from Bills and Parcels . "rules": { "tags": [], // up to 32 tag rules "sections": [], // up to 4 tabs and kinds "actions": [], // up to 12 buttons and menu lines "incoming": [] // up to 8 rules for texts as they come } (JSON has no comments: they're only to say what each is.) Each part may be left out, but a plugin needs at least one tag rule or one section ( empty_pack ). Conditions A condition, a rule's when or a section's takes , is an object whose keys are all optional. Every one given must hold. Key Holds when from The sender is one of these, 1 to 50 of them, each 3 to 64 characters. A number is compared by its digits alone, so +1 (555) 010-0100 and 15550100100 are the same; a name a company texts from is compared in any case. An entry with no digit or letter in it, such as (-) , matches nobody. tagged The text has every one of these tags, 1 to 8 of the plugin's own. untagged It has none of these, 1 to 8. setting A switch's key alone: that switch is on (its default until the person changes it). Or {"key": "level", "is": "loose"} : that choice is loose (its default until changed); for a switch, "is" is "on" or "off" . section Actions only: the conversation is in this section of the plugin's own, or "main" for Messages. Never true in a message's menu, which isn't in a section. Anywhere else it's section_condition . A plugin with an incoming rule can't use from anywhere ( from_with_incoming ): nobody can judge a rule that marks read or silences texts from numbers they don't know. Nor can a plugin with a link button ( bad_link_when ): a tag given by sender, a tab that takes by sender or that tab's row would offer the link for those numbers alone, and pressing it would tell the page which numbers wrote. In a tag rule, tagged and untagged see only the tags given by the rules before it, so naming a tag no earlier rule gives is unknown_tag . Everywhere else, a tag no rule gives is unknown_tag , and a section the plugin doesn't have is unknown_section . There's no condition on groups: a plugin never sees one. Tags A tag rule gives a text a tag when its words match. Several rules may give the same tag: they're different ways to get it. { "tag": "bill", "any": ["your bill is ready", "amount due {amount}"], "atLeast": 1, "none": ["unsubscribe"], "wordsFrom": "extra", "when": {"untagged": ["paid"]}, "detail": {"from": "token"} } Field What it is tag The tag it gives. Required. any 0 to 30 phrases , at least atLeast of which must match. atLeast 1 to 5, and 1 if left out. At most the number of any phrases, unless it has wordsFrom too. all 1 to 8 phrases that must all match. none 1 to 20 phrases none of which may match. wordsFrom A words setting's key: the words the person typed there join any , each a plain phrase ( their own words ). when A condition. detail What the tag keeps: words of your own (1 to 200 characters); {"from": "token"} , what a phrase's first token found; or {"from": "match"} , the whole of what a phrase matched. Nothing if left out. A rule needs something to start it: any , all , wordsFrom , or a when with from or tagged ( tag_rule_no_trigger ). How a text's tags are worked out For each text the plugin sees, its tag rules run in the order they're written, each one like this: If its when doesn't hold, with the tags given so far, the rule is passed over. Its phrases are its any , then the person's words from wordsFrom . If it has either, it counts how many of them match the text; fewer than atLeast , and it's passed over. A rule whose only phrases are the person's words does nothing until they type some. If it has all and one of them doesn't match, or none and one of them does, it's passed over. Its detail: your own words, if that's what it says; for {"from": "token"} , going through its phrases in order, what the first token found in the first phrase that has a token and matches; for {"from": "match"} , the whole match of the first phrase that matches. Trimmed, cut to 200 characters, and nothing where it's empty. The text gets the tag if it hasn't got it yet. If it has it already with no detail, and this rule found one, the detail is kept. Whenever one of the plugin's settings changes, every conversation's tags are worked out again. d: How a plugin finds words in a text: phrases, tokens like {digits:6}, and what a match gives it.
x: A plugin finds words in a text with phrases : plain words, like your bill is ready , with tokens where something varies, like amount due {amount} . There are no regular expressions and no code. The app turns each phrase into a search of its own making, with every repeat in it bounded, so a phrase can't run away with a phone however long or strange the text it reads. A phrase A phrase is 1 to 120 characters on one line, keeping the rules for words in a plugin . Read from left to right: { starts a token , which runs to the next } : a name, then optionally :N or :N-M . {digits:6} is {digits:6-6} , exactly six digits. {{ is a plain { , and }} a plain } . A run of spaces is one gap, which matches any run of space in the text: one space, several, a line break. Everything else is matched as it is: letters in any case, and every other character as itself. A . is a full stop, never "any character". The tokens Token Matches For example {digits:N-M} A run of N to M digits, not part of a longer run. 1 to 24, and 1-24 if you give no numbers. your code is {digits:4-8} finds 123456 in "Your code is 123456.", and nothing in "Your code is 1234567890". {number} A number: 1,234, 1.234,5, 98765 or 12.5. The whole run of digits, dots and commas it sits on, or nothing: 192.168.1.1 is no number. order {number} finds 1,234 in "Order 1,234 shipped". {amount} A number with a currency sign or code before or after it: $45.20, 45,00 EUR, £30. The signs are $, €, £, ¥ and ₹; the codes USD, EUR, GBP, CAD and AUD, in any case. amount due {amount} finds $1,234.56 in "Amount due $1,234.56 by Friday", and nothing in "Amount due 45 by Friday". {code:N-M} A whole word of N to M letters and digits with at least one digit in it. 4 to 24, and 4-10 if you give no numbers. code {code:4-8} finds AB12CD in "Use code AB12CD to sign in", and nothing in "Use code ABCDEF to sign in". {word} One word: letters, digits, ' and - . {word} delivery finds Acme in "Your Acme delivery is near". {words:N-M} N to M words of anything but spaces, between two plain parts of the phrase. 0 to 4, and 1-3 if you give no numbers. your {words:0-3} has shipped finds "new blue parcel" in "Your new blue parcel has shipped!" {url} A web address starting http:// , https:// or www. . track {url} finds https://example.com/t/123 in "track https://example.com/t/123 now". {email} An email address. from {email} finds bob.smith+x@mail.example.co.uk in "Reply from bob.smith+x@mail.example.co.uk." {phone} A phone number of 7 to 15 digits, with spaces, brackets, dots or dashes among them. The whole run it sits on, or nothing: two numbers with only a space between them read as one run. {phone} finds +1 (555) 010-0100 in "Call +1 (555) 010-0100 today". {date} A date: 12/03/2026, 2026-11-20, March 5th, 5 jan. Months are in English. on {date} finds March 5th in "Your appointment on March 5th at 3pm". {time} A time: 3pm, 10:30 a.m., 14:05. at {time} finds 10:30 a.m. in "See you at 10:30 a.m. sharp". The rules a phrase keeps A phrase that breaks one of these doesn't load, and says which at its place in the file ( rules.tags[0].any[2] ). They're checked in this order, and the first one broken is the problem given. Rule Broken by Problem Two tokens need something between them. {digits:4}{digits:4} phrase_tokens_touch A token can't touch a letter or digit. Punctuation may touch one: #{digits:4-10} and code:{code} are fine. bill{digits:4} phrase_token_touches_word {words} needs a space on each side, so it can't be first or last. {words:1-2} bill phrase_words_edge {url} must be followed by a space or the end of the phrase. {url}. phrase_url_followed At most 4 tokens, and only one {words} and one {url} among them. a {digits} b {digits} c {digits} d {digits} e {digits} phrase_too_many_tokens A phrase with no token needs at least two letters or digits. a phrase_too_short Besides those: a token the app doesn't know, numbers it can't take, a { with no } or a } on its own is phrase_bad_token ( {digits:0} , {digits:9-4} , {foo} , code {code:3} , go {words:5} , x {word:2} y , bill } ). An empty phrase, one over 120 characters, one with a space at its start or end, a line break or an invisible character is phrase_bad_text . How a phrase matches Whole words. A phrase that starts or ends with a letter or digit matches only whole words there: bill finds "bill" in "Your bill is ready", but nothing in "Your billing statement". Any case. Letters match in either case, accented ones too: your appt finds "YOUR APPT", and café finds "CAFÉ". Curly quotes and dashes. Before matching, the text and the phrase both have curly quotes made straight, dashes made - and odd spaces made plain ones, so don't forget finds "Don’t forget" written with a curly apostrophe. The first 2,000 characters of a text are read, and the rest isn't. The anchor. A phrase's longest run of plain letters and digits (a to z, 0 to 9), at least three long, is its anchor: the first, where two are as long. The phrase is only tried on a text that has its anchor in it, in any case, which is how hundreds of phrases stay quick. your code is {digits:4-8} 's anchor is your , and tracking no. {code:8-24} 's is tracking . A phrase with no such run, like {phone} , at {time} or café , is anchorless : it's tried on every text, so a plugin may have only 8. What a match gives A match gives two things: the whole of what the phrase matched, and what its first token found. A tag rule's detail keeps one of them for its tag, for a row or a copy button to show: {"from": "token"} : what the first token found. amount due: {amount} on "Amount due: 45,00 EUR." keeps 45,00 EUR. {"from": "match"} : the whole match. The same phrase keeps "Amount due: 45,00 EUR". Each is trimmed, and an empty one keeps nothing: your {words:0-3} has shipped matches "Your has shipped", with no detail. So a slow plugin is caught, and a phone that was only busy for a moment isn't held against it. More than 100 milliseconds of reading in any one second is a strike too, where its texts took it a millisecond or more each on average. The app reads every conversation again whenever a switch or a setting changes, and a plugin that's quick on each text isn't held against that. More than half of any one second spent reading is a strike however quick it is on each text, so a plugin that's nearly a millisecond a text can't hold the app for seconds every time a switch changes. The first text after it starts never counts: that's when its phrases are made ready. Five strikes in ten minutes pause it. It does nothing while paused, its page says Paused: it was slowing the app down. with Turn it back on , and the pause is kept, across restarts, until then or a new version. The person's own words A words setting lets the person type words of their own, a line each or with commas between. A tag rule's wordsFrom names that setting, and each of the first 50 entries, cut to 60 characters, becomes a phrase that joins the rule's any . Their words are taken as plain words: braces in them are plain braces, never tokens. d: What gets a plugin listed, what keeps one out, and how reports and withdrawals work.
x: Plugins in the Marketplace read people's texts, so they're held to more than working. These are what review looks for. Sending a plugin means saying, in the form, "I made this plugin, and it follows the Marketplace guidelines". What gets a plugin listed It does what it says. Its name, short line and description say what it does, and it does that and nothing else. Its phrases are precise. They match the texts it's for and not others. A phrase that's one short word, or a word like "your", catches far too much: Try the samples shows what yours catches, and a dinner plan or a sign-in code should come out untouched. What marks texts read or silences them is behind a setting , off until the person switches it on. The file format makes sure of that, so it's only a matter of saying clearly, in the setting's words, what it does. Its help link or email works , and reaches you. Its screenshots show it as it is , with made-up texts. Its words are plain. A description that says what it does, with no web addresses in it and no promises it can't keep. What keeps one out Another company's name, logo or marks anywhere in a plugin: its name, short line, description, tabs and kinds, faces, buttons, settings, icon or screenshots; or in your username or help address. A plugin that sorts a bank's texts can say "bank", not the bank's name. Looking like Ghost Messaging or a built-in plugin : its name, icon, colours or words. Screenshots showing real people's messages, names or numbers , yours included. Links to anything but your own pages. A plugin's one link is for its help or its own site. Anything hateful, sexual or harassing , in any of its words or pictures. Replies that aren't plain and polite. A button that writes a reply writes words the person sends as their own. Reports Anyone who has a plugin, or sees it in the Marketplace, can report it from its page with Report this plugin : why (it's misleading; it's harmful or abusive; it's spam; it asks too much of their texts; it doesn't work; or something else) and a few words. Their username goes with it only if they switch on Send my username with it . Every report is read, by a person, as soon as we can, and the harmful ones first. A report can lead to a plugin being taken off the Marketplace, a version being withdrawn, or its developer being blocked. Unlisting, withdrawing and blocking Unlisting takes a plugin off the Marketplace: nobody new can add it, and people who have it keep it. You can do it yourself from My submissions; review can do it too, and then only review can list it again. Withdrawing is for a version that should never have been approved. Every device that has it switches it off and says so ("Trips was withdrawn from the Marketplace and is off."), and its page gives the reviewer's reason: "Withdrawn from the Marketplace: … It's off, and does nothing until you remove it." It offers only Remove , and Update where a newer version is approved. The developer sees Withdrawn by review , with the same reason. An approved update doesn't withdraw the version before it unless review chooses to, so nobody's plugin stops working because they haven't updated yet. Blocking a developer stops them submitting ("This account can't submit plugins."), and may take their plugins off the Marketplace too.

d: What is sealed, what the server sees, blocking, reporting, and signing out.
x: Ghost Messaging is built so the people running its server can't read what you say. There are no ads, and the app is open source, so anyone can check. What's sealed end to end What Sealed end to end? Messages between friends, and in groups of friends Yes Circles and spaces: chat, files, polls Yes, with a key the circle's members share Calls Yes, between the people in them: through Ghost's relay, or directly where the relay can't be reached, still sealed Your texts with one person, with encryption on Yes Ordinary texts and picture messages No: they go through your carrier, as all texts do Telegram, Signal, WhatsApp and Matrix chats As those networks seal them; they go between your device and the network, not through Ghost What the server sees Which installs talk to each other, and when, as any server passing messages would. Your username, and your account backup sealed with your password (which it never sees). Your verified number, if you verify one, to text you codes. It's shown to nobody unless you choose. Never: what you write, your files, your recovery words or your password. On your device Spam filtering, sorting, translation, summaries, captions and transcripts all happen on your device. Your texts stay in your phone's own store. Plugins say on their pages what they can see. Plugins from other developers are reviewed before they're listed. They never see your contacts' texts, group texts, encrypted texts or your own (and nothing at all while Ghost Messaging can't read your contacts, since it couldn't tell them from strangers), and they have no way to send anything over the internet: a button you press can open the plugin's page in your browser or copy words to your clipboard. The Marketplace is fetched from our server, which sees your device's address and which plugins you add, and keeps no record of either. A report sends the plugin, what you chose and wrote, and your username only if you say so. A plugin you submit is listed with your username, help address and screenshots. Blocking and archiving Block someone from a conversation's menu or their card; a Ghost person when you report them. Settings › Archived (or Archive in the rail) has them; a new message brings one back. Reporting Report someone who sends spam, harasses you, pretends to be someone else or shares something illegal. Ghost doesn't scan anyone's messages: a report is how the team hears about it. A message: press and hold it in a chat with a friend, a group of friends, or a space, and choose Report . A person: open their card (tap their name or picture) and choose Report . Choose why, add a note if you like, and press Send report . Our server can't read your chats, so a message report takes the message and up to five messages either side of it with it, because you choose to hand them over. The report is sealed on your device so that only the Ghost Messaging reviewer can open it: the server keeps it without being able to read it.
